intro: Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak is an eight-verse devotional composition addressed to Hanuman, attributed to Tulsidas, the sixteenth-century poet-saint best known for the Ramcharitmanas. The word "ashtak" simply means a set of eight verses, and each verse here recalls a specific episode from Hanuman's life in which he faces a crisis, acts with courage or devotion, and resolves it. The refrain running through the text is a simple question - who in this world does not know Hanuman as the remover of troubles. Rather than offering abstract praise, the text builds its case for Hanuman's power through concrete stories: his childhood, his service to Sugriva, his search for Sita, his confrontation with Ravana's forces, and his role in saving Lakshmana's life. It is recited by devotees across India, particularly on days associated with Hanuman, as a way of recalling these episodes and invoking his presence.

groups.heading: The child who swallowed the sun
groups.body: The opening verse recalls an episode from Hanuman's infancy, when as a child he leapt toward the rising sun mistaking it for a fruit and swallowed it, plunging the three worlds into darkness. The verse describes the panic this caused and how no one could undo the situation until the gods themselves came and pleaded with him. Only then did he release the sun and restore light to the world. The verse closes with the refrain asking who does not know this monkey-hero as the one who removes calamity - setting up the pattern that each following verse will follow, naming a crisis and naming Hanuman as the one who met it.

groups.heading: Exile on the mountain and the sage's curse
groups.body: This verse turns to the period when Sugriva, afraid of his brother Bali, lived in hiding on a mountain, watching the path for any sign of threat. It recalls how a great sage, startled by apparent disrespect, pronounced a curse - the reasoning behind which the verse itself invites the listener to consider. It then recalls Hanuman appearing in the form of a learned brahmin to ease the distress of his master. The verse treats this as an example of Hanuman's resourcefulness and devotion, stepping in to resolve a difficult situation through wisdom rather than force.

groups.heading: The search for Sita with Angad
groups.body: Here Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak recounts the search party led by Hanuman and Angad, sent to find Sita after her abduction. The verse recalls the grim vow the search party made - that they would not return alive without news of her. It describes the party reaching the shore of the ocean, exhausted and without success, until word of Sita was finally brought back, restoring hope and, as the verse puts it, saving their lives. This section of the text is about perseverance under a self-imposed and dangerous deadline, and about the relief that came when the search finally succeeded.

groups.heading: Comforting Sita in Ashoka Vatika
groups.body: This verse moves to Lanka, where Sita is held captive and distressed by Ravana and threatened by the demonesses guarding her. It recalls how Hanuman, having crossed the ocean, enters the garden and kills a powerful demon sent against him. The verse then describes Sita's despair - her readiness to end her life by fire - and how Hanuman hands her Rama's ring as a token, easing her sorrow and giving her proof that help has come. The verse frames this moment as one of reassurance delivered at the point of greatest despair.

groups.heading: Lakshmana's wound and the healing herb
groups.body: The final verse of the stotra describes the battlefield crisis when Lakshmana is struck by a weapon and falls unconscious, after Rama's forces have already killed Ravana's son Meghnad. It recalls the physician Sushena's advice, and Hanuman's journey to bring back the entire Dronagiri mountain because he could not identify the single herb needed. The verse closes with the healing herb restoring Lakshmana's life, framed once more by the refrain praising Hanuman as the one who removes the gravest of troubles. This verse is often considered the emotional high point of the text.

groups.heading: The repeated refrain and its place in the text
groups.body: Each of the eight verses of the stotra ends with the same line, asking rhetorically who in this world does not know Hanuman by this name - the remover of difficulty. This repetition is not incidental; it is the structural spine of the composition. Every story told in the preceding lines exists to justify this one claim, building it episode by episode rather than asserting it outright. Readers familiar with the Ramcharitmanas will recognise these episodes as drawn from that larger narrative, compressed here into a focused, devotional sequence meant for repetition rather than for telling the story in full.

recitation: Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak is traditionally recited on Tuesdays and Saturdays, the two days of the week commonly associated with Hanuman worship, and especially on Hanuman Jayanti. Many devotees recite it as part of a daily or weekly practice, often after reciting the Hanuman Chalisa, in the early morning or evening at a Hanuman temple or at a home altar with a lit diya and incense. There is no single prescribed count for this particular text the way there is for some mantras; it is usually read once or a few times in a sitting, with attention given to understanding the meaning of each verse rather than to repetition for its own sake. Some devotees read it silently, others aloud, and in many temples it is recited collectively during evening aarti gatherings. The tradition holds that the text is well suited to being read slowly, episode by episode, since each verse stands as a separate recollection rather than a continuous narrative. As with most stotras, there is no single correct way to recite it - what is generally emphasised is sincerity and a clear understanding of what is being recalled, rather than speed or exact ritual form.
tradition: Within the devotional tradition surrounding Hanuman, Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak is regarded as a text of comfort recited in moments of difficulty, drawing its authority from the very name it repeats - Sankat Mochan, the remover of difficulty. The tradition holds that reciting it is a way of remembering how Hanuman responded to crises faced by others, from Sugriva to Sita to Lakshmana, and of drawing on that memory for steadiness rather than expecting a specific result. Because it is attributed to Tulsidas, it is also read as part of the wider devotional literature connected to the Ramcharitmanas, and is often recited alongside the Hanuman Chalisa, which is also attributed to the same poet. Temples dedicated to Hanuman, including the well-known Sankat Mochan temple in Varanasi, are closely associated with this text and its themes, though the text itself does not claim to guarantee any outcome - it is presented by tradition as an act of remembrance and devotion.

faq.q: What does "Sankat Mochan" mean in the title?
faq.a: Sankat means difficulty or crisis, and Mochan means one who removes or releases. Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak can be understood as "eight verses to Hanuman, the remover of difficulty" - a title that reflects the refrain repeated at the end of each verse in the text.

faq.q: Is Sankat Mochan Hanuman Ashtak the same as the Hanuman Chalisa?
faq.a: No, they are different compositions, though both are attributed to Tulsidas and both are devoted to Hanuman. The Chalisa has forty verses covering a broader range of praise, while this text has eight verses, each tied to a specific episode from Hanuman's life. Many devotees recite both, often one after the other.

faq.q: On which days is it usually recited?
faq.a: Tradition associates Tuesdays and Saturdays with Hanuman worship, and these are the most common days for reciting the stotra. It is also widely recited on Hanuman Jayanti, the day marking Hanuman's birth, and during other Hanuman-related observances through the year.

faq.q: Does the text need to be recited in Sanskrit pronunciation rules like a mantra?
faq.a: It is composed in Awadhi, not Sanskrit, and is generally treated as devotional poetry rather than a mantra requiring strict phonetic precision. The emphasis in tradition is on reciting it with understanding and sincerity rather than on exact ritual pronunciation.

faq.q: Can it be read by anyone, or are there restrictions?
faq.a: There is no widely recorded restriction on who may read the stotra. It is commonly recited by people of all ages, at home or in temples, individually or in groups, and is considered accessible devotional literature within the broader Hanuman worship tradition.
